title.en: Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic and Neutral

text.en: Two labelled cups contain dilute lemon solution and mild soap solution. Their contents look similar. The teacher places a strip beside each cup to compare how the samples change its colour.

Lemon juice and vinegar are familiar acidic substances. A solution of baking soda is basic. We can test and classify the samples by the changes they cause in an indicator. Use indicators to test teacher-provided samples. Do not taste or touch a sample to try to identify it.
An indicator changes colour in acids and bases. Litmus paper turns from blue to red in acid and from red to blue in base. Yellow turmeric turns reddish brown in a basic solution. Red rose extract is another natural indicator and can look red with an acid and green with a base. A neutral substance, like pure water, does not change the colour of litmus.
Acids are used in food and in cleaning. Bases are used in soaps and antacids. When an acid reacts with a base in neutralisation, salt and water can form and heat can be released. The amounts used affect whether any acid or base remains. The textbook uses an acidic ant sting to illustrate why an acid and a base can react. We will investigate that chemistry using labelled samples on the classroom bench.

Set a blue strip and a red strip beside pictures of three cups. Use them to compare familiar samples. An indicator gives us an observable clue about a substance.
First try the dilute lemon sample in the demonstration. The blue strip turns red and the red strip stays red. Both observations fit an acidic sample.
With a dilute baking soda solution, red litmus turns blue but blue litmus stays blue. This is what we expect from a basic sample.
Test the container of pure water with both fresh strips. Both keep their starting colours. Under the conditions of this test, that fits a neutral sample.
If only the red strip stays red, you still have two possibilities. The liquid may be acidic or neutral. A fresh blue strip can help you decide which it is.
Use separate clean droppers for each sample. Leftover lemon solution could turn blue litmus red in the next cup and make your result difficult to interpret.
Picture a teacher showing red rose extract in three clear cups. Each starts with some of the same extract. Keep one unchanged so you have an original colour to compare.
Compare the rose extract after adding the acidic sample and the basic sample. The first can show a shade of red, while the second can look green. Record the observed colours beside the labels.
Start with a yellow turmeric paper. A drop of basic solution creates a reddish brown patch. A drop of dilute vinegar on another fresh piece leaves it yellow.
Pure water also leaves this turmeric paper yellow. Turmeric helps identify a base, but we need another test to distinguish these acidic and neutral samples.
Suppose paper treated with turmeric shows reddish marks only where a teacher drew with mild soap solution. The marks show where the soap solution changed the colour of the indicator.

board.text: Reddish marks show where the basic sample touched

text.en: A chart helps you compare tests side by side. Put the sample in the first column and your observations in the next columns. Add the classification only after you read the results.
A dark sample can make an indicator colour hard to see. Say that the result is unclear and compare it with a suitable fresh strip or another indicator chosen by your teacher.
Turn to a teacher demonstration. Begin with a dilute acidic sample whose indicator shows the acid colour. The teacher adds a dilute base in small amounts and checks how the indicator changes.

board.text: Observe while the teacher adds a base

text.en: As the acid and base react, less of the original acid remains. If more base is added than the acid can react with, the final mixture can become basic.

board.text: Extra base can leave a basic mixture

text.en: In a class example with suitable amounts, the acid and base react to form a salt and water. Neutralisation can also release heat. A teacher can observe that safely with an instrument.

Bring the idea to a water treatment plant. Engineers test an acidic wastewater stream and control how it is treated before further checks. An indicator reading is evidence about acidity, not proof that water is safe.

board.text: Treatment involves testing and further checks

text.en: A farmer can ask for a soil test before deciding what treatment a field needs. Crops differ in the conditions they grow in, and a soil test gives more information than guessing from the colour of the soil.
Imagine a label that says a medicine is an antacid. The chemistry idea behind the name is that a basic ingredient can react with acid. In our class, we model that idea with sample cups.

board.text: A basic ingredient can react with acid

text.en: Sort two imaginary samples. Sample A turns blue litmus red. Sample B turns red litmus blue. Explain which observation you used for each conclusion.
What if your turmeric paper stays yellow for a clear sample? Write two possible classifications and choose which fresh test can separate those possibilities.
Finish by choosing an indicator and explaining how you would use a comparison. Name one observation that supports your conclusion and one result that would leave you unsure.

problem.en: Blue litmus turns red in a solution. What is it?

text.en: Blue litmus turns red in acid.
So the solution is acidic.

prompt.en: Explain why we should not taste substances to find out if they are acidic.

requiredIdeas.en: An indicator offers an observable test without tasting the sample.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking all sour things are the same strength.

points.en: Classify substances using colour changes in suitable indicators.
Litmus: acid turns blue to red; base turns red to blue.
